clue.text: Gentleman full of love giving away ring — it's precious

indicators.note: the title is full of the other letters, holding them inside

parts.note: SIR is the form of address for a gentleman

indicators.note: giving something away means losing it, so a letter leaves the word love

parts.note: taken as written before a letter is removed
the round letter O looks like a ring

explanation.surface: A gentleman who has broken off an engagement is left with something precious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'giving away' means losing, so love drops its O; 'full of' then puts what is left inside the title, between its I and R.
explanation.definitionFit: Silver is one of the precious metals, prized for jewellery and coinage.

clue.text: Charlie and I had one set of books

parts.note: I had contracts to I'd, giving ID
the Roman numeral for one is I
OT is the Old Testament, a set of books of the Bible

explanation.surface: Someone named Charlie and the speaker shared a set of books.
explanation.walkthrough: Charlie is British slang for a fool, as in 'a right Charlie'.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling someone a Charlie is British slang for saying they are a fool.

clue.text: After six look around entrance to institute — requirement for guard

indicators.note: the next letters come after the numeral in the answer

parts.note: VI is six in Roman numerals

indicators.note: the word for look goes around the other letter

parts.note: a glance is a quick look

indicators.note: the entrance to a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: After six o'clock, a guard checks the entrance to an institute, as the job demands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' puts I, the first letter of institute, inside GLANCE after its G.
explanation.definitionFit: Watchfulness is what a guard needs most: keeping alert for any danger.

clue.text: Traveller to pass away after travel is cut short

indicators.note: the word for dying follows the shortened word for travel
the word for travel loses its last letter

parts.note: to roam is to travel about
to die is to pass away

explanation.surface: A traveller worries about dying after a journey is curtailed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is cut short' takes the M off ROAM to leave ROA.
explanation.definitionFit: A roadie travels with a touring band, setting up its equipment at each venue.

clue.text: Ladies maybe in place where spa water is available?

definitions.meaning: the Ladies is a public lavatory, one kind of washroom

definitions.text: place where spa water is available?
definitions.meaning: Bath is an English spa city

explanation.surface: A spa's water can be had in the Ladies, it seems.
explanation.walkthrough: Bath is a Somerset city famous for its Roman spa waters; the question mark flags the punning second reading.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ladies is a women's lavatory, which polite usage often calls a washroom with a toilet.

clue.text: Hides ten benches needing repair out of sight

indicators.note: something needing repair is broken, so these letters must be put back together differently

explanation.surface: Someone hides ten broken benches where nobody will see them.
explanation.definitionFit: What happens away from the audience's view takes place off stage, hidden from the public.

clue.text: Hurling an object? Quarrel must be contained

indicators.note: the quarrel must be held inside the word for object

parts.note: a thing is an object
a row is a quarrel

explanation.surface: Someone throws an object, and the resulting quarrel needs to be kept in check.
explanation.definitionFit: Hurling something is the act of flinging it with force.

clue.text: Not all are belligerent, subversive

indicators.note: Not all says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Some, though not everyone, are aggressive and seditious.
explanation.definitionFit: A subversive is someone working to undermine authority, an insurgent against it.

clue.text: Players roar after foul play outside the box

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go on the outside of the word for box
foul play suggests the word roar has been interfered with, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: a chest is a box

explanation.surface: Footballers roar after a foul outside the penalty box.
explanation.walkthrough: 'foul play' and 'the box' suggest football, but the players are musicians. 'after foul play' rearranges the letters of roar, and 'outside' wraps them around the word for box.
explanation.definitionFit: An orchestra is a body of musicians, players who perform together.

clue.text: Creator of life in a bookshop?

definitions.text: Creator of life in a bookshop?

parts.words: Creator of life in a bookshop?
parts.note: not a god but a writer whose books, found in a bookshop, tell the story of someone's life

explanation.surface: Who creates life among the shelves of a bookshop?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Creator of life' suggests a deity; the bookshop shows the life is a written account.
explanation.definitionFit: This writer produces life stories of real people, the books that are sold in a bookshop.

clue.text: Father of twenty children, unmarried man neglecting half!

indicators.note: half of the eight letters are left off, keeping only the first four

parts.note: a bachelor is an unmarried man

explanation.surface: A father of twenty children, or a bachelor who neglects half of them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'neglecting half' drops ELOR, the second half of the word for unmarried man.
explanation.definitionFit: Johann Sebastian, the composer, fathered twenty children across his two marriages.

clue.text: Horse in stable needed by one riding

indicators.note: the word for stable is followed by the next pieces

parts.note: a stall is a compartment in a stable
one in Roman numerals is I
riding on a horse, so riding gives ON

explanation.surface: A horse in its stall is needed by someone who wants to ride.
explanation.definitionFit: A stallion is an uncastrated male horse, often kept for breeding.

clue.text: It's ineffective, carrying everything in case

indicators.note: the word for ineffective carries the other word inside it

parts.note: wet is British slang for feeble or ineffective
all means everything

explanation.surface: It's useless lugging everything around in one case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wet' is British slang for feeble or ineffectual, as of a timid person.
explanation.definitionFit: A wallet is a small folding case for banknotes and cards.

clue.text: Avoid bypass — waste of time

indicators.note: wasting the time letter means it is lost from the word

parts.note: to shunt is to sidetrack or divert, bypassing something

explanation.surface: Steer clear of the bypass road: it wastes time.
explanation.definitionFit: To shun someone is to keep away from them deliberately.

clue.text: A shock? One may go through it for the better

definitions.text: A shock? One may go through it for the better

parts.words: A shock? One may go through it for the better
parts.note: a shock is a thick mass of hair; the grooming tool drawn through it improves its look

explanation.surface: A sudden shock that someone goes through may change them for the better.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shock' looks like a jolt, but a shock of hair is a thick unruly mop.
explanation.definitionFit: This bristled tool is pulled through a mop of hair to tidy it.

clue.text: This mint sacked moneymaker? Probably not

indicators.note: sacked suggests something plundered and thrown into disorder, so the letters are scattered

explanation.surface: This mint was ransacked; was its coin-maker responsible? Probably not.
explanation.walkthrough: A mint makes money, but this metalworker makes pots and pans from tin, so 'Probably not' qualifies the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A worker in tin plate is a metal craftsman, not a minter of coins.

clue.text: Beggar to stop in middle of busy road on slope

indicators.note: the word for stop goes in the middle of the road's letters

parts.note: the M1 is a busy British motorway, written MI
to end is to stop
cant is a slope or tilt

explanation.surface: A beggar tries to stop traffic in the middle of a busy road on a hill.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is the motorway from London to Yorkshire; its 1 is read as I.
explanation.definitionFit: A mendicant lives by begging, like the mendicant friars of old.

clue.text: Spent a whole season or a short day outside Bury

indicators.note: the short day goes outside the word for bury

parts.note: WED is short for Wednesday, a day of the week
to inter is to bury

explanation.surface: Someone stayed in Bury, the Lancashire town, for a whole season or just a short day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bury' looks like the Lancashire town; it is the verb, INTER.
explanation.definitionFit: To winter somewhere is to pass the cold months there.

clue.text: Similarly resembling Ernie, being comical?

parts.note: like means resembling
Ernie Wise was the comedian partnered with Eric Morecambe

explanation.surface: Similarly, it resembled Ernie, being funny.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being comical' points to Ernie Wise of Morecambe and Wise, a much-loved British comedy double act.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something in the same way as others is doing it in a similar fashion.

clue.text: Bird heading west, not very close

indicators.note: in an across clue, heading west means reading right to left
not says the following abbreviation is missing

parts.note: a raven is a bird

explanation.surface: A bird flying west is not very near.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not very' drops V from RAVEN to leave RAEN; 'heading west' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: Close and near both describe something at only a short distance.

clue.text: Chum we had upset in a flap

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means turned upside down

parts.note: a pal is a chum
D is the contraction of had, as in I'd

explanation.surface: A friend we knew was upset and in a flap.
explanation.definitionFit: A dewlap is a fold of loose skin hanging from the throat of cattle or dogs.

clue.text: Inattentive sailor discharged?

parts.note: AB is an able seaman
sent means dispatched or discharged

explanation.surface: A sailor who has been discharged is no longer paying attention.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone absent-minded or with an absent look is not paying attention.

clue.text: Some people ate rare piece of fruit?

indicators.note: only some of the letters of these words are used, a run inside them

explanation.surface: Some diners ate their meat rare, followed by fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: An eater is an apple for eating raw, as opposed to a cooker; the question mark marks the stretch.

clue.text: Devon town with distinction, getting on

parts.note: a credit is a grade of distinction in an exam

explanation.surface: A Devon town getting on with distinction.
explanation.walkthrough: Crediton is a market town in Devon, a county in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Crediton is a small market town in mid-Devon, north-west of Exeter.

clue.text: The end, nothing very big

parts.note: O, the figure zero, means nothing
mega is slang for huge

explanation.surface: The finale was nothing very impressive.
explanation.walkthrough: Omega is the last letter of the Greek alphabet, hence 'the end'.
explanation.definitionFit: As the final Greek letter, omega stands for the last of anything.

clue.text: It's only fair

definitions.meaning: only in the sense of merely or barely
fair in the sense of equitable or right

explanation.surface: It's only fair, after all.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both merely, as in only a moment, and fair, as in a righteous verdict.

clue.text: Chief of crooks spinning grander lie

indicators.note: spinning sends the letters round so they come out in a new order

explanation.surface: The boss of a gang spins an ever bigger lie.
explanation.definitionFit: The head of a criminal gang is the one who organises the others in wrongdoing.

clue.text: Absurd activities with some in Paris at back of old coach

indicators.note: the French word goes at the back of the coach letters

parts.note: chara is a short form of charabanc, an early open motor coach
des is French for some

explanation.surface: Silly activities with some people in Paris at the back of an old coach.
explanation.walkthrough: A charabanc, often shortened to chara, was an early open motor coach used for British seaside outings.
explanation.definitionFit: Pretences that are obviously absurd are called a farce or pantomime: things done for show.

clue.text: Route taken by an Asian

parts.note: a path is a route

explanation.surface: A route taken by an Asian traveller.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pathans, or Pashtuns, are a people of Afghanistan and Pakistan.
